question: The Greek and European peach compote industries are threatened by imports from China (under CN 2008.70), which increased by 44 % in the period from 2020 to 2023 and amounted to 47 600 tonnes in the first four months of 2025 alone. With an average price of EUR 1.04/kg, or even EUR 0.80/kg in some regions, these imports are being sold at prices below the costs of Chinese producers themselves (EUR 0.95/kg to EUR 1.

15/kg). This phenomenon is the result of a state-led dumping strategy, which includes subsidies, VAT refunds and low energy and labour costs. European production costs (EUR 1.17/kg to EUR 1.27/kg) make it impossible to compete without making a loss. Employing 20 000 families and exporting 98 % of production, the sector is a mainstay of the Central Macedonian and European agri-food industry.

Although institutional tools are available, the Commission has not imposed anti-dumping measures, as it has done for related products (mandarins, sweetcorn) with duties of up to EUR 531/tonne. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it intend to open a preliminary anti-dumping investigation into imports of Chinese compote (CN 2008.70) with the possibility of retroactive measures?
How will it ensure equal treatment with other agricultural sectors?
Will it consider updated tariffs and enhanced monitoring of imports to maintain the sustainability and self-reliance of the European canned fruit sector?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.1.2026) The Commission is fully committed to protecting EU industries from unfair competition from imports. At present, the EU has over 220 trade defence measures in place, including on foodstuffs such as citrus fruits from China1 and sweetcorn from Thailand2 both currently subject to expiry reviews.

There is also an ongoing anti-dumping investigation on sweetcorn from China3. The Commission conducts investigations where it receives evidence from any EU industry that it is suffering from dumped and/or subsidised imports and that action is warranted. Any industry can contact the Commission’s trade defence services4 to discuss such issues.

The Commission imposes anti-dumping and/or countervailing measures once an investigation has found that injurious dumping or subsidisation is taking place, and it is in the EU interest to do so. There can be both provisional and definitive measures imposed.

Moreover, where several legal conditions are met, definitive anti-dumping duty may be levied on products which were entered for consumption before no more than 90 days prior to the date of application of provisional measures, provided those imports were registered. However, this is a decision that is made only at the end of an investigation.
Measures can be subject to review and can be maintained for as long as is necessary to ensure the protection of an industry from unfairly traded imports.
